clinicalPearls: A rare, potentially sight-threatening inflammation of the sclera posterior to the equator, often with minimal or absent anterior signs so it is easily missed.
Pain is typically severe, deep and boring, worse on eye movement, and may radiate to the brow, jaw or temple with globe tenderness.
It may produce proptosis, diplopia and restricted ocular motility, mimicking orbital disease.
B-scan ultrasonography is the key investigation, showing scleral and choroidal thickening with fluid tracking into the sub-Tenon space producing the T-sign.
Posterior segment signs include exudative retinal detachment, choroidal folds, disc oedema, uveal effusion, macular oedema and a subretinal mass mimicking a tumour.
Around half of cases are associated with a systemic autoimmune disease such as rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, lupus, relapsing polychondritis or IgG4-related disease.
Management is graded by severity, using systemic non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, corticosteroids and steroid-sparing immunosuppression or biologics.
Infective and masquerade causes should be excluded before committing to immunosuppression.
reference.pathophysiology: Posterior scleritis is an immune-mediated inflammation of the collagen-rich posterior sclera, frequently occurring as an ocular manifestation of systemic autoimmune or vasculitic disease. Immune-complex deposition and cell-mediated hypersensitivity drive inflammatory infiltration and oedema that thicken the sclera and track into the sub-Tenon space and adjacent choroid. This produces the characteristic ultrasonographic findings and secondary changes such as choroidal effusion, exudative retinal detachment and disc swelling.
additionalDifferentials: Orbital inflammatory disease or orbital cellulitis
Choroidal tumour such as melanoma or metastasis
additionalInvestigations: B-scan ultrasonography seeking scleral thickening and the T-sign
Optical coherence tomography to demonstrate subretinal fluid and choroidal folds
Magnetic resonance imaging or computed tomography of the orbits when orbital or mass pathology is suspected
Inflammatory and autoimmune serology including full blood count, ESR, CRP, ANA, ANCA, rheumatoid factor and angiotensin-converting enzyme
Infective screen for syphilis and tuberculosis before starting immunosuppression
redFlags: Severe pain accompanied by significant visual loss
Proptosis with restricted motility raising concern for orbital cellulitis
Systemic features suggesting an underlying vasculitis
A subretinal or choroidal mass raising suspicion of malignancy
reference.prognosis: The outlook is generally good when treatment is prompt and appropriately intensive, though recurrences occur and any associated systemic disease influences overall outcome. Delayed recognition and treatment risk permanent visual loss.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosis as orbital cellulitis or a choroidal tumour leading to inappropriate management
Overlooking the diagnosis in a painful eye with a normal anterior segment
Failing to investigate for an associated systemic autoimmune disorder
Commencing corticosteroids without first excluding an infective cause
references: American Academy of Ophthalmology, Basic and Clinical Science Course, Uveitis and Ocular Inflammation
management: Treat with systemic corticosteroids as the mainstay, by oral or intravenous route according to severity, to control the scleral inflammation
Add non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs in milder disease and for adjunctive symptom control
Introduce steroid-sparing immunosuppression such as methotrexate or mycophenolate, or a biologic such as an anti-TNF agent or rituximab, for refractory or recurrent disease
Exclude infective mimics including syphilis and tuberculosis before starting immunosuppression
Investigate and co-manage any associated systemic autoimmune disease (rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, lupus, relapsing polychondritis, IgG4-related disease) with rheumatology
Monitor treatment response with B-scan ultrasonography and optical coherence tomography, watching for exudative retinal detachment and macular oedema
Treat promptly and escalate immunosuppression for recurrence to prevent permanent visual loss
